title: How Much Does Prior Knowledge Really Matter for Learning
author: Carl Hendrick
summary: Carl Hendrick works through a new experimental study by Zachary Buchin and Neil Mulligan that tested the 'knowledge is power' hypothesis and found no benefit of prior domain knowledge for learning a new topic in that domain. He takes the finding seriously, acknowledging that the design is rigorous and that it exposes a real methodological flaw: most prior-knowledge studies measure the stability of individual differences rather than new learning, and a meta-analysis using gain scores found essentially zero correlation. He then argues the results should be read with caution, chiefly because three days of training produces recent exposure rather than consolidated, interconnected schemas. He adds concerns about topic interconnection, ecological validity, and a possible interaction in which prior knowledge makes retrieval practice feel easier and so removes its desirable difficulty. His conclusion reframes rather than rejects the study: knowledge supports learning only when it is structured, stable and deeply integrated over time.
points: The Buchin and Mulligan study found no advantage in final scores, learning gains or retrieval performance for learning a new topic within a domain participants had just trained in, even though learners reported it felt easier.

Hendrick's main objection is that three days of training and a 36-hour gap cannot produce schema formation, so the study measured recent exposure rather than prior knowledge in any meaningful educational sense.

He credits the researchers' gain-score critique, noting a meta-analytic correlation of essentially zero (r = -.06) between prior knowledge and new learning, which suggests much earlier research measured pre-existing differences rather than learning.
He speculates that prior knowledge may reduce the effortful difficulty that makes retrieval practice work, or that its benefits combined with retrieval may only show over weeks rather than 48 hours.
His reframing is that the study refines rather than refutes the knowledge-is-power hypothesis: the structure, coherence and consolidation of knowledge are what matter.
quotes: One of the foundational assumptions in the science of learning is that prior knowledge facilitates new learning. It's an idea so widely accepted that it's often considered self-evident: the more you know, the more you can know.

This is a surprising and frankly unsettling finding. If Ausubel’s above axiom is true (that prior knowledge is the single most important factor in learning) then we would expect at least some measurable advantage when students approach new material in a domain they’ve just trained in.
The most fundamental issue for me is that participants received just 3 days of training. This isn't really "prior knowledge" in any meaningful educational sense. It's more like recent exposure.

When high-knowledge students perform better on final tests, it might just reflect that they were already better, not that they learned more. The meta-analysis finding is striking: when properly assessed with gain scores, the correlation between prior knowledge and new learning was essentially zero (r = -.06). This suggests decades of research may have been measuring the wrong thing.

Every teacher knows that real-world learning involves problem-solving, application, and messy integration across contexts. Paradoxically, prior knowledge benefits might be most apparent when students don’t recall the knowledge verbatim, but when they need to apply that knowledge flexibly, not just recall facts.

However, when participants possess relevant domain knowledge, this interaction becomes theoretically complex and potentially problematic for interpreting the results. If prior knowledge makes retrieval practice feel easier (as the mental effort ratings suggest), this could paradoxically reduce the very difficulty that makes retrieval practice effective.

Schema-based learning doesn’t happen overnight, and knowledge that isn't richly interconnected may offer little advantage for transfer or extension. So perhaps this study isn’t a refutation of the knowledge-is-power hypothesis, but a refinement: knowledge supports learning only when it’s structured, stable, and deeply integrated.
